The salt spray crusted on Elias’s windows, turning the world outside into a blurred watercolor of grays and blues. Inside, the air hummed with the rhythmic, mechanical heartbeat of the Fresnel lens, rotating slowly, casting its beam across the churning Atlantic. For forty years, Elias had been the silent guardian of Blackwood Point, a solitary sentinel against the relentless tide.

Tonight, the storm was particularly vicious. The wind howled like a wounded beast, rattling the iron stairs that spiraled up to the lantern room. Elias adjusted his woolen coat, his arthritic knees protesting with every step. He wasn’t just maintaining the light; he was maintaining order in a chaotic universe. The ships below were invisible specks in the dark, relying entirely on his vigilance. If the lens failed, if the oil ran dry, or if his own heart simply stopped, lives would be lost. The weight of that responsibility was heavier than the iron door he had just closed.
